passage: Monday, 8:45, in the dispatch office. Vijay stood at the whiteboard and wrote three lines: sign the courier contract, finish the training plan, clear the backlog of invoices. Neelam came over with her own list, fourteen lines long, and raised an eyebrow. “Fourteen never gets finished,” Vijay said. “Three might.” Each evening at six Vijay ticked what was done and rubbed out nothing. On Wednesday a truck broke down and ate the whole afternoon, so the invoices slipped. By Friday the contract was signed and the training plan was sent, and beside the invoices Vijay wrote “Monday, first”. Neelam copied the three-line idea onto a sticky note that evening.

qa.q: What three outcomes did Vijay write on the whiteboard?
qa.a: Vijay wrote: sign the courier contract, finish the training plan, and clear the backlog of invoices.

qa.q: What does Vijay's calm explanation to Neelam show about Vijay's view of long lists?
qa.a: Vijay feels that a long list weighs people down and rarely gets finished, and prefers three lines that might really be done.

qa.q: What went wrong on Wednesday, and how did Vijay handle it?
qa.a: A truck broke down and took the afternoon, so the invoices slipped; Vijay simply moved them to “Monday, first” instead of abandoning the list.

qa.q: Why might Neelam have copied the three-line idea onto a sticky note?
qa.a: Neelam may feel weighed down by fourteen items and is impressed that Vijay's short list survived a bad day.

grounding: A wise planner picks three outcomes for the week, writes them down and checks them every evening.

passage:
Dear Ishita,

You asked how I stop the week running away from me. On Sunday evening I take a small card and write three outcomes, not tasks, that would make the week a good one: the vendor quote sent, the leave roster fixed, my mother's papers filed. Then I stick it on the monitor. Every evening I look at it for two minutes and tick what moved. Last week the quote and the roster got done; the papers did not, and I moved them to next week without a fuss. Before I used the card, I kept a list of twenty things and felt guilty by Tuesday. Try it for two weeks and write back.

Lalit

qa.q: Where does Lalit stick the card?
qa.a: Lalit sticks the card on the monitor.

qa.q: How did Lalit feel about the old twenty-item list?
qa.a: Lalit felt guilty by Tuesday, because twenty things could not be finished and the list only piled up blame.

qa.q: What did Lalit do when the mother's papers were not filed?
qa.a: Lalit moved the papers to next week without fuss and kept the card going.

qa.q: Why might Ishita have asked Lalit about running away weeks?
qa.a: Ishita probably feels swamped by too many tasks and hopes for a simple method, so a small card may feel doable. 🙂

grounding: A wise planner chooses three weekly outcomes, writes them down and reviews them each evening; short lists survive real days.

passage: People ask how I stopped drowning at work. I'm Anirban. Two years ago my to-do list had forty-one items. Every night I'd look at it and feel sick. My flatmate Santosh watched me one Sunday and said, "Just pick three things for the week. Only three." I laughed, but I tried it. First week: finish the vendor report, call Baba about his tests, run twice. I wrote them on an index card and stuck it by the kettle. Every evening I looked at it while the water boiled. By Friday two were done and the run happened once. That felt like winning, not failing.

qa.q: How many items did Anirban's to-do list once have?
qa.a: Anirban's to-do list had forty-one items.

qa.q: How did Anirban feel about his long list before he tried the top three?
qa.a: Anirban felt sick and overwhelmed looking at it every night.

qa.q: Which part of Anirban's method makes the evening check easy?
qa.a: Sticking the index card by the kettle meant Anirban saw the three outcomes every evening while the water boiled, without needing to remember.

qa.q: How might Santosh see the change in Anirban?
qa.a: Santosh probably feels pleased and a bit proud that the simple advice helped Anirban stop feeling crushed by work.

grounding: Illustrates a young adult choosing three important outcomes for the week, writing them down and checking them each evening.

passage: I share an office with Eshaan at the logistics firm, and I've noticed a change since spring. Every Monday at nine he takes a yellow card and writes three lines. I once saw it: "Ship Pune order. Fix invoice error. Mentor Preeti." Every evening before leaving, he looks at the card, ticks something or frowns, and puts it back under his keyboard. His desk used to be buried in sticky notes. Now it's mostly clear. Preeti told me he gave her a full hour on Wednesday, the first time anyone had. I can't know how he feels inside, but he seems calmer.

qa.q: Where does Eshaan keep his yellow card?
qa.a: He puts it back under his keyboard.

qa.q: What might Eshaan be feeling now that he uses the three-line card?
qa.a: He seems calmer and more in control, judging by his clear desk and steady evening check.

qa.q: What could the colleague try if they want the same results?
qa.a: They could write their own three outcomes on Monday and check them each evening, instead of keeping many sticky notes.

qa.q: How is Preeti affected by Eshaan's new habit?
qa.a: Preeti benefits directly, getting a full hour of mentoring on Wednesday because she was one of his three priorities.

grounding: An observer describes a colleague who picks three weekly outcomes, writes them down and checks them each evening.

passage:
Monday. Chetan's notebook held a list of twenty-two tasks for the week at the bank branch. By Tuesday night he had crossed off six small ones and none of the big ones. He felt heavy.
Wednesday. Zeenat, his team lead, showed him her card: three outcomes, nothing else. That evening Chetan tore out a fresh page and wrote: close the loan file audit, train the new cashier, send the quarterly report. He checked it before sleeping and moved one step forward on each.
Next Monday. Chetan wrote three new lines. By Friday all three had ticks, and the long list felt less like guilt.

qa.q: How many tasks were on Chetan's first list?
qa.a: Chetan's notebook held a list of twenty-two tasks for the week.

qa.q: What was Chetan feeling on Tuesday night?
qa.a: He felt heavy and discouraged because he had only crossed off small tasks and none of the big ones.

qa.q: Which change worked for Chetan, and why?
qa.a: Writing only three outcomes and checking them each evening kept his attention on what mattered, so all three were done the next week.

qa.q: How might Zeenat see Chetan's progress?
qa.a: Zeenat would likely feel pleased that sharing her simple card helped her team member finish the important work.

grounding: Shows over days how a young worker moves from a long list to three weekly outcomes checked each evening.

passage:
Yogesh, you're always telling me your to-do list is two pages long. Let me, your Vishal chacha, tell you how I survived my first year running the trucks.
I had four trucks, six drivers and one phone. Every day, forty small fires. I'd make long lists at night and wake up feeling guilty because I never finished half.
An old transporter in Nagpur, Bhatia-ji, laughed at my list. "On Sunday night, write three things. Only three. What must be true by Saturday?"
So I did. One week it was: get the insurance renewed, collect the pending payment from the mill, fix truck two's brakes. Every evening I looked at those three lines. If I'd moved them forward, I slept. The other forty fires still came, but I handled them around the three.
By the end of that year, I had six trucks.
The long list is only guilt, beta. Three things, and look at them every evening.

qa.q: How many trucks did Vishal have at first?
qa.a: I had four trucks.

qa.q: How did young Vishal feel after making long lists at night?
qa.a: Vishal woke up feeling guilty, because he never finished even half of the long lists.

qa.q: What choice in the story changed how Vishal managed his week?
qa.a: Following Bhatia-ji's advice to write only three must-do outcomes each Sunday and check them every evening.

qa.q: How might Bhatia-ji have felt seeing young Vishal's two-page list?
qa.a: Bhatia-ji seemed amused but kind, laughing at the list and offering simpler advice.

grounding: An elder recalls replacing long guilty to-do lists with three weekly outcomes checked every evening.
